The 2026 selection 01 – 06

6 essential apps for a trip to Japan.

Less “now what?”
More “look at this place”.

Kanjidon Team · Updated September 2026

Your digital luggage↗

さあ！

The flight is booked. You’ve already saved more restaurants than you have meals planned. Now there’s one thing left: getting your phone ready. These are the six apps we’d put in our “Japan” folder in 2026, to help you get around, make sense of what’s in front of you and enjoy the trip. Starting on the plane.

In this guide

Six apps.
One trip.
So much to discover.

For finding your way

1. Google Maps

01

The ramen’s here. The entrance? Less obvious.

You’ve saved a little ramen spot, a wonderful bookshop and a hotel that looked so easy to find. Google Maps is where they all come together: addresses, directions, photos and reviews, all on the same map.

The trick for Japan is to start using it before you leave. Create a list for each city, add the places that catch your eye and share it with your travel companions. Once you’re there, open the map and see what’s nearby. Including that café you’d completely forgotten about.

Know before you go

Download maps of the areas you’ll be visiting. You’ll still need a connection to get walking and public transport directions.

App Store↗Google Play↗
Official information ↗

For trains and the metro

2. Japan Travel by NAVITIME

02

Connections, platforms, timetables. Breathe.

Google Maps helps you explore. NAVITIME earns its place alongside it when you start piecing together trains, metro journeys and trips between cities: it shows connections, timetables and platform information. It’s designed specifically for travelling in Japan and is available in English.

The feature to look out for? Routes for Japan Rail Pass holders. You can also organise your stops into an itinerary, instead of rebuilding your plan from fifteen screenshots every morning. Your Kyoto day trip will thank you.

Know before you go

The basic features are free; some, such as finding alternative routes during service disruptions, require a paid plan.

App Store↗Google Play↗
Official information ↗

For understanding and asking

3. ChatGPT

03

“Okay, but what actually is this dish?”

Take a photo of the menu, upload it and ask: “Translate these dishes and explain what they are.” With ChatGPT, you can keep the conversation going: ask about a name, find a polite way to order or make sense of a sign. The best part is being able to ask the next question.

A tip? Be specific about the context. “I’m in a little restaurant in Osaka: how do I ask if I can pay by card, simply and politely?” is much more useful than “translate pay”. You can even practise out loud before going in. Then it’s over to you.

Know before you go

You’ll need a connection. Image and voice usage limits depend on your plan; send clear photos and double-check important names and numbers.

App Store↗Google Play↗
Official information ↗

For setting off with a little Japanese

4. Kanjidon

04

Wait. I can read that!

Arriving in Japan and recognising a character, a word, a little piece of what’s in front of you feels amazing. Sounds like a small thing? Wait until it happens.

You can start with the basics: hiragana, katakana, kanji and vocabulary. Then come quizzes, illustrated cards to collect and stories: “I’ll just do five minutes” starts taking an interesting turn. You build some familiarity with Japanese while having fun, without turning your travel prep into a second job.

And if you like a challenge, there’s the League and Live too. Download it a few days before you leave: your first souvenir could be a word you can already read.

Know before you go

Even on the plane, you can do quizzes and review offline using content already available on your phone. Open the app and get everything ready before take-off.

App Store↗Google Play↗
Official information ↗

For getting connected

5. Airalo

05

Land. Connect. Send “I’m here”.

As soon as you land, you want three things: to let everyone back home know, find the train and work out where you put your passport. For the first two, an internet connection helps a lot. Airalo lets you buy and manage a Japan eSIM, without physically swapping your SIM.

Choose a data package based on the length of your trip and how much you expect to use. The advantage is getting ready at your own pace, instead of starting your holiday hunting for Wi-Fi. Then maps, translations and bookings are all a tap away again.

Know before you go

You’ll need an eSIM-compatible, carrier-unlocked phone. Check the package duration and activation conditions: data-only plans don’t include a number for calls and texts.

App Store↗Google Play↗
Official information ↗

For calling a taxi

6. GO

06

Eventually, your legs get a vote too.

You’ve been walking all day. It’s raining. Your suitcase has decided to become gym equipment. This is when you’re glad you downloaded GO: set your pickup point and destination, then request a taxi in the app.

It’s one of Japan’s go-to taxi apps and features in GO TOKYO’s official selection too. It supports English, registration with overseas phone numbers and international credit cards. A great plan B when walking suddenly loses all its appeal.

Know before you go

Download it beforehand; finish signing up in Japan with SMS verification. Before confirming a ride, check the dispatch charges and any extra fees for international visitors.

App Store↗Google Play↗
Official information ↗

Now for the good part

6 tips. Then Japan, here we come.

The apps are ready. Now put them to work: one small move with each, and your holiday starts looking even better.

  1. Google Maps↗

    Build a plan B worth getting excited about.

    Make a “Japan, if it rains” list of cafés, museums and bookshops you’d love to visit. Open it at the first downpour: you might end up in your favourite place of the whole trip.

  2. NAVITIME↗

    Sort the return trip. Then go exploring.

    Before a day trip, check the connections back too and take a screenshot of the timetable. The sunset is beautiful. The last train leaving without you? Less so.

  3. ChatGPT↗

    Take a phrase of your own to dinner.

    Upload a photo of the menu and ask: “How do I order this dish simply and politely? Write the sentence in Japanese, its pronunciation and its meaning.” Practise it out loud. Then look up and use it.

  4. Kanjidon↗

    Let the kanji hunt begin.

    Pick three characters from your collection, practise them in quizzes and try spotting them on signs, menus and packaging. When you recognise one out on the street, that little “I know this!” feels huge.

  5. Airalo↗

    Save your data for the detours.

    Choose a package for the length of your trip and keep track of usage in the app. Download films and playlists over Wi-Fi before leaving: save your data for maps, messages and changes of plan.

  6. GO↗

    Make yourself easy to find.

    Choose an easy-to-spot pickup point, such as your hotel entrance, and check the pin on the map. When the taxi arrives, match its vehicle number with the one shown in the app.

Now go fill your camera roll with photos, your suitcase with unlikely purchases and your head with “I have to come back here”. Japan, we’re really on our way.

Selected by Kanjidon Team and checked against official websites and app store listings on 5 September 2026. The apps are available for iOS and Android; features and prices may change. Kanjidon is developed by our team.

Sources and selection details
